name: Muon optimizer for hidden 2-D matrices (AdamW kept for embeddings/head/1-D params)
current: Single AdamW over all params (lr 2e-3, wd 0.1 on >=2D incl. tied embedding), betas default (0.9,0.999).
proposal: Hybrid optimizer: Muon (SGD-Nesterov momentum 0.95 -> Newton-Schulz-5 orthogonalization) for all 2-D weights inside Blocks (q/k/v, attn proj, MLP fc/proj). AdamW (betas 0.9,0.95) for the tied token embedding/lm_head, position embedding, LayerNorm params and biases. Muon effective lr ≈ 0.02 (or Moonlight-style 0.2*sqrt(max(m,n)) RMS matching with the AdamW lr).
mechanism: Orthogonalizing the momentum equalizes singular values of each update, amplifying rare directions that AdamW's update under-weights. That gives more loss decrease per token. This matters here because the token budget is fixed and the model is still improving at the end of training.

evidence.source: Keller Jordan, 'Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks' (blog)
evidence.finding: Muon sets the NanoGPT/FineWeb speedrun records, a 1.35x speedup over AdamW at 124M. It is applied only to hidden 2-D params; embeddings, head and scalars stay on AdamW. NS coefficients (3.4445,-4.7750,2.0315), 5 steps, Nesterov momentum.

evidence.source: Liu et al., 'Muon is Scalable for LLM Training' (Moonlight)
evidence.finding: With weight decay and per-parameter update-RMS matching to AdamW, Muon is ~2x more sample-efficient than AdamW in compute-optimal scaling-law runs.

expected_effect: Largest single expected gain: roughly −0.05 to −0.12 nats of val loss at an equal token budget (speedrun evidence ≈ AdamW needing 1.35x+ more tokens).
applicability: The evidence is from 124M-and-up models on FineWeb, the same data family as here. Hidden matrices are small (256×256 and 256×1024), so NS-5 in fp32 costs <2% of step time. The non-embedding part is only 4.8M params, so the gain may be smaller than at 124M because AdamW still handles the dominant embedding table.
risks: The training loop overwrites every group's lr, so the Muon lr must be derived via a per-group multiplier. Too high a Muon lr with no QK-norm can cause logit growth. In fp32, NS needs normalization by the Frobenius norm first.
implementation: In build_optimizer: hidden=[p for n,p in model.named_parameters() if p.dim()==2 and 'blocks.' in n]; others split into decay/no-decay AdamW groups. Write a class Hybrid(torch.optim.Optimizer) holding groups tagged {'muon':True,'lr_mult':10}. In step(), for Muon groups: buf=state.momentum_buffer; buf.mul_(0.95).add_(g); g=g.add(buf,alpha=0.95) (nesterov); X=g/(g.norm()+1e-7); transpose if rows>cols; for _ in 5: A=X@X.T; B=b*A+c*A@A; X=a*X+B@X; scale by max(1,rows/cols)**0.5; p.mul_(1-lr*wd); p.add_(X,alpha=-lr*lr_mult). For AdamW groups, run a standard Adam update inline (or hold an internal torch AdamW and copy lr). Keep lr=2e-3 for the Adam parts, Muon lr = 0.02 (lr_mult 10); sweep lr_mult 5–20.

name: RoPE + QK-norm in a fused multi-head attention (drop learned absolute positions)
current: Learned absolute position table added to token embeddings. Per-head Python loop of separate Linears. Manual softmax path in eval (a different code path from training). No normalization of q/k.
proposal: Single qkv Linear(n_embd,3*n_embd) reshaped to (B,H,T,hd). Apply RMSNorm (or F.rms_norm) to q and k per head, then rotary embeddings (base 10000) to q,k, then F.scaled_dot_product_attention(is_causal=True) in both train and eval. Remove position_embedding_table and pos_emb add.
mechanism: RoPE injects relative position into q·k, which is a better inductive bias than an additive learned table at T=128 and frees the residual stream. QK-norm bounds attention logits, which stabilizes training and tolerates higher LR (it pairs well with Muon). Fusing the heads removes 3×H small matmuls per layer, which also improves throughput.

evidence.source: Su et al., RoFormer
evidence.finding: RoPE encodes absolute position by rotation with explicit relative dependency; now standard in Llama/OLMo/SmolLM and the modded-nanoGPT recipes.

evidence.source: Wortsman et al., Small-scale proxies for large-scale Transformer training instabilities
evidence.finding: qk-layernorm prevents attention-logit growth and enables stable training across ~3 orders of magnitude of LR, shown with small models.

evidence.source: OLMo 2 Furious
evidence.finding: QK-norm (with other norm changes) improved training stability and loss in OLMo 2.

expected_effect: ≈ −0.02 to −0.05 nats; a higher usable peak LR; a 10–25% throughput gain from fusing, which buys time headroom for other changes.
applicability: Pure architecture change with a slight parameter decrease (−32K). The ingredients are standard at every scale, including the 124M speedrun. Fusing uses SDPA, which is available in fp32 on an L4.
risks: The RoPE implementation must use correct pairing and cache cos/sin for T≤128. QK-norm removes implicit temperature learning; add a learnable gain or keep the default scale. Some code logs attention_values/embedding tensors, so keep attrs or guard them.
implementation: MultiHeadAttention.__init__: self.qkv=nn.Linear(C,3C,bias=False); self.proj=nn.Linear(C,C); hd=C//H; inv=1/(10000**(torch.arange(0,hd,2)/hd)); t=torch.arange(block_size); f=torch.outer(t,inv); register_buffer cos=f.cos(), sin=f.sin(). forward: q,k,v=self.qkv(x).view(B,T,3,H,hd).unbind(2); q,k=F.rms_norm(q,(hd,)),F.rms_norm(k,(hd,)); rotate: x1,x2=x[...,::2]... or half-split: y=cat(x1*cos-x2*sin, x1*sin+x2*cos); transpose to (B,H,T,hd); y=F.scaled_dot_product_attention(q,k,v,is_causal=True); proj. Keep Head class unused or delete. In forward_body: x=tok_emb (no pos_emb); keep position_embedding_table out of model_init.

name: ReLU² (or param-matched SwiGLU) MLP
proposal: Option A (modded-nanoGPT style): same shapes, activation F.relu(x).square(), bias=False, zero-init the output projection. Option B: SwiGLU with hidden = 683 (≈ 8/3·C, param-matched): w2(silu(w1 x) * w3 x).
mechanism: Squared ReLU and gated units give sharper, sparser feature selection and a better loss per FLOP than GELU in language-model FFNs. Both are drop-ins with equal parameter count.

evidence.source: So et al., Primer
evidence.finding: Squared-ReLU is one of the two modifications responsible for most of Primer's gains; it cuts training cost up to 4x combined with dconv, and the benefit is robust across scales and codebases.

evidence.source: Shazeer, GLU Variants Improve Transformer
evidence.finding: GEGLU/SwiGLU give the best perplexities vs ReLU/GELU FFNs at matched params/compute.

applicability: Parameter-neutral and cheap. ReLU² is what the current modded-nanoGPT speedrun (small FineWeb models) uses. SwiGLU is used in every Llama-family small model (TinyLlama, SmolLM).
risks: ReLU² can produce larger activations. That is fine with pre-norm, but pair it with zero/small-init output projections. SwiGLU at hidden 683 adds one more matmul and slightly lowers throughput.
implementation: FeedForward: self.fc=nn.Linear(C,4C,bias=False); self.proj=nn.Linear(4C,C,bias=False); init_weights: nn.init.zeros_(self.proj.weight) (or xavier*0.5). forward: h=F.relu(self.fc(x)).square(); self.gelu_activation=h.detach() (keep attr for logging); return self.dropout(self.proj(h)). SwiGLU variant: w1,w3=Linear(C,683), w2=Linear(683,C); return w2(F.silu(w1(x))*w3(x)).

name: Linear decay-to-zero (D2Z) LR schedule
current: Linear warmup 300 steps, then cosine from 2e-3 down to min_lr 2e-6.
proposal: Linear warmup (300 steps, or ~2% of steps), then decay linearly to 0 over the rest (min_lr=0). Optionally, a WSD variant: hold the peak until 70–80% of steps, then decay linearly to 0.
mechanism: Viewing AdamW as an EMA of weight updates, linear D2Z balances early movement away from init against late averaging of gradient noise better than cosine does. Cosine spends too long at low LR and too little at mid LR.

evidence.source: Bergsma et al., Straight to Zero: Why Linearly Decaying the LR to Zero Works Best for LLMs
evidence.finding: Linear D2Z consistently beats cosine (10x decay) across model sizes, batch sizes and datasets. The advantage grows with tokens-per-parameter; 610M at 80 TPP with D2Z beat 200 TPP with 10x decay.

expected_effect: ≈ −0.005 to −0.02 nats. Small but nearly free.
applicability: The current cosine already reaches ~0, so the gain comes only from the shape (more time at mid-range LR). The run's 6.9 TPP is low, and the paper found smaller gains at low TPP. That makes this a low-risk polish that stacks with the other cards.
risks: Minor. If combined with Muon, apply the same multiplier schedule to both parts.
implementation: lr_at_step: warmup unchanged; after warmup: progress=(step-warmup)/(total-warmup) clamped; return min_lr + (lr-min_lr)*(1-progress). Set min_lr=0.0. WSD option: if progress<0.75: return lr; else return lr*(1-(progress-0.75)/0.25).
trigger: Manual validation run (M7): audit the current best program for outdated or missing techniques.

name: Spend freed wall-clock on depth: deep-thin 8–10 layers (bolder)
current: 6 layers × 256 wide, 4 heads. Only 4.8M non-embedding params, 27% of the total. The run takes 2898 s of a ~3660 s cap.
proposal: After fusing attention (card 2), raise n_layer to 8 (~19.3M params; +1.58M) or 10 if throughput allows, keeping n_embd=256 and n_head=4 (head dim 64).
mechanism: Loss mostly tracks non-embedding capacity. Here the lm_head/embedding (12.9M) dominates FLOPs, so each extra block costs only ~5% more compute yet adds ~33% more non-embedding capacity per two layers. At sub-billion scale, depth beats width.

evidence.source: Liu et al., MobileLLM: Optimizing Sub-billion Parameter LMs
evidence.finding: At 125M/350M, deep-and-thin architectures (e.g. 30 layers instead of 12) with embedding sharing gave a +2.7%/4.3% accuracy boost over prior same-size models.

expected_effect: ≈ −0.02 to −0.05 nats if the run stays within the time cap.
applicability: The parameter cap (26.5M) allows up to ~12 layers. The binding constraint is time. The current per-head loop wastes throughput, and fusing likely recovers enough for +2 to +4 layers in fp32 on an L4.
risks: Wall-clock overrun (check tok/s in a screen run first). The evidence is at 125M+, larger than here. The model is already under-trained at 6.9 TPP, so returns from extra depth may be smaller.
implementation: Hyperparameter change: n_layer=8 (try 10 if tok/s ≥ ~40k after card 2). Keep everything else fixed. Estimated time = 122.88M / measured tok/s; must be < ~3500 s including eval.
trigger: Manual validation run (M7): audit the current best program for outdated or missing techniques.

name: Retune weight decay (and floor) for the 3-epoch data-repetition regime
current: AdamW weight_decay=0.1, the single-pass default. The run makes about 3 passes over 40.5M tokens. The val−train gap is 0.263 and grew by +0.018 over the last 20% of training.
proposal: Sweep weight_decay over {0.2, 0.3, 0.5}, starting with 0.3, and keep everything else as in p3. Decay still applies only to 2-D weights, which include the tied embedding/head. If 0.3 wins, also try 0.5 (the top of the allowed range).
mechanism: When data repeats, the model starts memorising sequences it has already seen. Decoupled weight decay shrinks the weight norm and acts as the main working regulariser. Recent data-constrained studies find the best weight decay grows with epoch count and sits well above 0.1. At lr 3e-3, each step's shrink is lr×wd, so 0.3 gives about 9e-4 per step at peak, and it vanishes as the LR decays.

evidence.source: Data-Constrained LM Pretraining: Improved Regularization and Scaling Laws
evidence.finding: Strong weight decay is critical under data repetition. Tuned values run 0.4 to 3.2 (versus the standard 0.1) for 72M–1.4B models, with AdamW (β2=0.95) and dropout 0.1.

evidence.source: Pre-training under infinite compute (Kim et al.)
evidence.finding: With data limited and multiple epochs, the best weight decay is about 30× larger than standard practice.

evidence.source: Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models (Muennighoff et al.)
evidence.finding: Up to about 4 epochs costs little versus unique data. So the gain from regularisation at 3 epochs will be modest but real.

expected_effect: About −0.01 to −0.04 val loss. The gap should shrink and the loss curve in the final phase should be smoother.
applicability: Changes one hyperparameter at zero cost. The 3-epoch, 6.9 tokens/param regime is exactly the one these papers study, although their evidence comes from more epochs and larger models, so the best value here is probably lower (0.2–0.5).
risks: Too much decay shrinks the tied embedding table, where most parameters live, and can underfit. If 0.5 hurts, back off. It interacts with the LR: raise the LR later and the per-step shrink grows with it.
implementation: Hyperparameter only: weight_decay=0.3 (the sweep's first point); no code change needed. Optional second step: exclude the token embedding from decay if the tied table is found to over-shrink. In build_optimizer: decay_params = [p for n,p in model.named_parameters() if p.dim()>=2 and 'token_embedding' not in n], with the embedding at weight_decay 0.0.

name: GPT-2/modded-nanogpt init: std-0.02 hidden weights plus zero-initialised residual output projections
current: All linear layers use Xavier (uniform, or normal in each Head). With in=256 and out=64, that gives std ≈ 0.079 for q/k/v. The attention output projection and the MLP down-projection are also Xavier, with no depth scaling. So each block writes a full-magnitude update into the residual stream from step 0.
proposal: Init q/k/v and the MLP up-projection as normal(0, 0.02). Zero-init the attention output projection (sa.proj.weight) and the MLP down-projection (net[2].weight), and set all linear biases to zero. The fallback, if zero-init stalls, is GPT-2's std 0.02/sqrt(2·n_layer) for those two projections.
mechanism: With zero-init output projections, every block starts as the identity. The residual stream then carries the clean embedding at init, and each block learns only the update it needs. This is the 'muP-like' zero init from modded-nanogpt and the same idea as GPT-2's 1/sqrt(2L) residual scaling. It keeps activation variance from growing with depth, so a high LR (3e-3) is safer, early loss falls faster, and there are fewer spikes (p3 had 3).

evidence.source: modded-nanogpt README (Keller Jordan et al.)
evidence.finding: Record 5 (Oct 2024) added zero-init projections together with ReLU² and QK-norm. Those 'modern architecture' changes cut the 124M speedrun from 22.3 to 15.2 minutes. Zero-init has stayed in every later record.

evidence.source: GPT-2 / nanoGPT init (Radford et al. 2019; Karpathy nanoGPT)
evidence.finding: Weights are normal(0, 0.02), and residual output projections are scaled by 1/sqrt(2·n_layer). This is the standard small-GPT init.

expected_effect: About −0.01 to −0.03 val loss, mostly from faster early progress and more stable high-LR training.
applicability: Costs nothing and involves only init code. It works at every scale, including the 6-layer, 256-wide model here. It fits naturally with the higher LR adopted in p3.
risks: Setting q and k both to zero would kill gradients, so only zero the output projections. Head.init_weights and MultiHeadAttention.init_weights run after the generic loop, so they must be edited or they will overwrite the new init.
implementation: In the attention block: Head.init_weights sets nn.init.normal_(w, 0, 0.02) for key, query and value. MultiHeadAttention.init_weights: nn.init.zeros_(self.proj.weight); nn.init.zeros_(self.proj.bias). In the mlp block, add FeedForward.init_weights(self): nn.init.normal_(self.net[0].weight, 0, 0.02); nn.init.zeros_(self.net[0].bias); nn.init.zeros_(self.net[2].weight); nn.init.zeros_(self.net[2].bias). model_init already calls every submodule's init_weights after the Xavier default, so no other change is needed. Keep the token embedding at std 0.02.

name: Tanh logit soft-cap on the tied LM head (and drop the 50k-entry head bias)
component: model_init (lm_head), attention block for class def
current: logits = lm_head(ln_f(x)), with the head tied to the embedding and an unregularised 50,257-entry bias. Nothing bounds the logits, even with a high 3e-3 LR over repeated data.
proposal: Replace lm_head with a Linear subclass whose forward returns cap·tanh(logits/cap), with cap=15 (modded-nanogpt's current value; also try 30, Gemma 2's value). Build it with bias=False, so the tied head carries no separate bias.
mechanism: The soft-cap stops the model from pushing logits to extreme values, a form of over-confidence that shows up especially on repeated data. It gently limits the logit scale, much like z-loss, which reduces loss spikes and memorisation of frequent tokens. The loss stays smooth near zero because tanh(x)≈x for small logits.

evidence.source: modded-nanogpt README
evidence.finding: Record 9 added a logit softcap of 30, following Gemma 2. Record 18 lowered it from 30 to 15 and got a measurable further speedup on 124M FineWeb.

evidence.source: Gemma 2 technical report
evidence.finding: Final logits are soft-capped at 30 with cap·tanh(x/cap) to stabilise training.

expected_effect: About −0.005 to −0.02 val loss and fewer spikes. It removes 50,257 parameters.
applicability: Costs little: one tanh over (B,T,V) logits, which is small next to the head matmul. Works with fp32 and weight tying. The evidence comes from 124M models on FineWeb, a close match to this data.
risks: A cap that is too low (under 10) can hurt calibration and loss for a 50k vocabulary. Check that the bias-free Linear is created before the tying line and that nothing still references lm_head.bias.
implementation:
In the attention block (module level), add: class SoftcapLinear(nn.Linear):
    def __init__(self, i, o, cap=15.0): super().__init__(i, o, bias=False); self.cap = cap
    def forward(self, x): return self.cap * torch.tanh(F.linear(x, self.weight) / self.cap)
In model_init, set self.lm_head = SoftcapLinear(n_embd, vocab_size, cap=15.0). Delete the nn.init.constant_(self.lm_head.bias, 0) line, but keep tying: self.lm_head.weight = self.token_embedding_table.weight. Tying happens after init_weights, so the Xavier loop cannot overwrite the tied weight.

name: Value residual learning (ResFormer): mix layer-1 values into every later layer (bolder)
current: Standard attention: each layer's values come only from its own input. Nothing connects the first layer's token-level values to later layers.
proposal: Keep the layer-0 value tensor v1 (per head). In every later layer n, use v_n' = λ_n·v_n + (1−λ_n)·v1, with λ_n a learnable scalar per layer initialised to 0.5. This adds only n_layer parameters.
mechanism: Deeper layers tend to lose token-identity information: attention concentrates on 'sink' tokens and the values sent to them drain toward zero. A shortcut from the first layer's values, which have no such drain, restores that information and weakens the loop between attention sinks and drained values. modded-nanogpt uses a close cousin (value skips and value embeddings).

evidence.source: Value Residual Learning (Zhou et al., arXiv 2410.17897)
evidence.finding: ResFormer reaches the same val loss as a Transformer with 16.1% fewer parameters and 20.3% less data, at about equal compute and memory.

evidence.source: modded-nanogpt README
evidence.finding: Record 9 introduced value and embedding skip connections, and records 14–15 added value embeddings. These were among the larger speedups in the 124M speedrun.

expected_effect: About −0.01 to −0.03 val loss if the paper's data-efficiency gain carries over. The gain may be smaller with only 6 layers.
applicability: Adds almost no compute or parameters. The evidence comes from 82M+ models and from modded-nanogpt at 124M; no one has shown it at 5M non-embedding parameters, which makes it the bolder idea. Full value embeddings would add about 12.9M parameters each and break the cap, so use the plain value residual.
risks: Adds plumbing across three blocks, where bugs can happen. The gain may be small at depth 6. It must work with the SDPA training path and the eval path, which are currently different code paths.
implementation: Head.forward(x, v1=None, lam=None): v = self.value(x); if v1 is None: v1_out = v; else: v = lam*v + (1-lam)*v1; v1_out = v1. Use this v in both the SDPA path and the eval path, and return (out, v1_out). MultiHeadAttention.forward(x, v1s=None, lam=None) loops over the heads and collects the per-head v1s. Block adds self.lam = nn.Parameter(torch.tensor(0.5)) and forward(x, v1s=None): a, v1s = self.sa(self.ln1(x), v1s, self.lam if v1s is not None else None); x = x + a; x = x + self.ffwd(self.ln2(x)); return x, v1s. In forward_body: v1s=None; for block in self.blocks: x, v1s = block(x, v1s). The 1-D lam falls into the no-decay group automatically.

name: Light dropout for the repeated-data regime (0.05–0.1)
current: dropout=0.0 everywhere, with 3 epochs over 40.5M tokens and a 0.26 val−train gap that is still growing late in training.
proposal: Try dropout=0.05, then 0.1. Keep the existing placement: after the embedding, after the attention and MLP outputs, and on attention probabilities via SDPA's dropout_p. Test separately from card 1 before combining.
mechanism: On the second and third passes, the model sees the same sequences again. Dropout adds noise so that each pass acts like a slightly different example, which limits memorisation. For language models the benefit seems to come from regularisation during repeats rather than from the classic co-adaptation story.

evidence.source: To Repeat or Not To Repeat (Xue et al., NeurIPS 2023)
evidence.finding: Multi-epoch training degrades performance through overfitting. Of the regularisers tested, only dropout helped substantially, though it needs tuning.

evidence.source: STLM Engineering Report: Dropout (arXiv 2409.05423)
evidence.finding: In models under 100M parameters, dropout stays effective when overfitting, and can help even with plenty of data.

expected_effect: Uncertain: somewhere between −0.02 and +0.02. It helps if the growing gap reflects real overfitting, and hurts if the model is still underfitting at about 6.9 tokens/param.
applicability: Hyperparameter only. With only 3 epochs, the repeated-data papers predict mild overfitting, so keep the rate small. Being small also limits slowdown on the SDPA path.
risks: Dropout slows convergence, and the run is flagged 'still_improving'. It may cost more than it saves. The rate of 0.3 used in older recipes is far too high here. Run this after the weight-decay test, since both target the same gap.
implementation: Set hyperparameter dropout=0.05; the code already routes it through the embedding dropout, SDPA dropout_p, the projection and the MLP. If it helps, try 0.1. Optional refinement: in Head.forward pass dropout_p=0.0 to SDPA, keeping only residual dropout, which reduces the slowdown.

name: Hashed bigram input embedding using the spare ~8.8M parameter budget
current: The input is tok_emb + pos_emb from a single 50257×256 table tied to the LM head. 8.84M parameters of the cap are unused.
proposal: Add an untied, input-only embedding table indexed by a hash of (previous token, current token): 32,768 rows × 256 = 8.39M params, total about 26.07M, under the cap. Zero-init it. Add it to x at the input with a learnable scalar, and optionally re-inject it before every block with per-layer scalars initialised to 0.1, as in modded-nanogpt.
mechanism: Much of the loss for a small LM comes from local n-gram statistics. A direct bigram lookup gives these to the model for free, so the few non-embedding parameters (4.8M) can go to longer-range structure. Only the input vocabulary grows. The output softmax does not change, so this avoids the harm that larger output vocabularies do to small models. The compute cost is one gather.

evidence.source: modded-nanogpt PR #201: Bigram Hash Embedding record
evidence.finding: Table of 5×vocab rows, hash xor(36313*cur, 27191*prev) % mod, zero init, added through per-layer bigram_lambdas initialised to 0.1. Steps to target fell from 1765 to 1600 (about 9%), a new world record.

evidence.source: Huang et al., Over-Tokenized Transformer: Vocabulary is Generally Worth Scaling (arXiv 2501.16975)
evidence.finding: Summing hashed 1-, 2- and 3-gram input embeddings gives loss that falls log-linearly with input-vocabulary size, from 151M models upward. Growing only the input vocabulary helps small models, while a larger output vocabulary hurts them.

expected_effect: Probably a large gain for this regime, roughly 0.03–0.10 nats of val loss, because the model is small and most of its loss is local statistics. Throughput should barely change.
applicability: The parameter cap counts parameters, not FLOPs, and embedding lookups are almost free. This is the cheapest way to use the 8.8M unused parameters. 40M tokens × 3 epochs visit each frequent bigram many times.
risks: Rare bigrams may be memorised over 3 epochs; keep weight decay on the table. Hash collisions add noise. Position 0 of each crop has no previous token, so use a sentinel id. Using 32,768 rows × 256 must stay under the cap: 17,683,281 + 8,388,608 + a few scalars ≈ 26.07M.
implementation:
In __init__: self.bigram_emb = nn.Embedding(32768, n_embd); nn.init.zeros_ in init_weights. Make sure the generic init does not overwrite it: it is an Embedding, not a Linear, so it is safe. self.bigram_lambdas = nn.Parameter(0.1*torch.ones(n_layer)).
In forward: prev = torch.cat([torch.full_like(idx[:, :1], 50256), idx[:, :-1]], 1); h = ((36313*idx) ^ (27191*prev)) % 32767 (use int64); xb = self.bigram_emb(h). Then x = tok_emb + pos_emb + xb. For the richer variant, inside the loop: x = x + self.bigram_lambdas[i]*xb before block i. The 1-D lambdas land in the no-decay group automatically; the 2-D table is decayed.

name: Canon layers: residual causal depthwise conv (kernel 4) inside each block (bolder)
current: Tokens mix only through softmax attention. Nothing in the model is cheap, local and position-aware.
proposal: In every block, apply a causal depthwise Conv1d with kernel 4 as a residual to the attention input: h = ln1(x); h = h + canon(h); x = x + sa(h). Optionally add the same before the MLP (Canon-C). Initialise the conv weights small, e.g. std 0.02 or zeros.
mechanism: The conv gives each token a learnable weighted sum of its last 3 neighbours, so attention heads no longer have to spend capacity on previous-token and induction-style local lookups. The paper finds this doubles effective reasoning depth and lets weak positional schemes (NoPE) match RoPE. modded-nanogpt's 'smear' gate is a kernel-2 version of the same idea.

evidence.source: Allen-Zhu, Physics of Language Models Part 4.1: Architecture Design and the Magic of Canon Layers (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2512.17351)
evidence.finding: Canon layers are trainable 1-D causal convs with kernel 4 and a residual, adding about 0.5% params. They improve reasoning depth (about 2×) and breadth, and lift NoPE to RoPE level. Shown in synthetic tasks and in academic-scale real pretraining.

evidence.source: modded-nanogpt (smear module)
evidence.finding: A sigmoid-gated 'smear' of the previous token into the current one was adopted in the speedrun record line, which shows that cheap local token mixing helps GPT-2-small training.

expected_effect: About 0.01–0.04 nats of val loss, and about 0.2% more parameters (6 × 256 × 4 weights).
applicability: The context is only 128 tokens and the model has 4 heads × 6 layers, so attention capacity is scarce. Offloading local mixing is most valuable in exactly this setting. It runs fine in fp32 on an L4.
risks: Real-data gains at tens of millions of params are less documented than the synthetic results. A wrong pad direction leaks future tokens: pad left only and verify causality. The conv adds a little time.
implementation:
In Block.__init__: self.canon = nn.Conv1d(n_embd, n_embd, 4, groups=n_embd, bias=False); nn.init.normal_(self.canon.weight, std=0.02).
In forward: h = self.ln1(x); c = F.pad(h.transpose(1,2), (3,0)); h = h + self.canon(c).transpose(1,2); x = x + self.sa(h); x = x + self.ffwd(self.ln2(x)).
The conv weight is 3-D, so it goes into the decay group. Consider moving it to the no-decay group.

name: Learnable x0 re-injection + U-net skip scalars (modded-nanogpt residual lambdas)
current: A plain residual stream, where each block only adds its output to x.
proposal: Keep x0 = the embedding sum. Before block i, set x = a_i*x + b_i*x0 with learnable scalars a_i = 1 and b_i = 0 (or 0.1). Add U-net skips as well: store block outputs from the first half and add them, each scaled by a learnable scalar initialised to 1 (or 0.5), to the inputs of the mirrored later blocks. With 6 layers, use pairs 0→5, 1→4, 2→3.
mechanism: Every layer gets direct access to the token identity and a short gradient path to the embeddings. U-net skips let later layers reuse early features and partly bypass middle layers. Both add only a handful of scalars.

evidence.source: snimu, modded-nanogpt: Analyzing value-embedding-, UNet-, and x0-lambdas
evidence.finding: The x0 formula is x = x_lambda*x + x0_lambda*x0 per layer, and the U-net skip lambdas are initialised to 1. Trained models keep substantial skip weight (about 20% skipping of middle layers), so the skips are really used.

evidence.source: LessWrong: How the NanoGPT speedrun WR dropped by 20% in 3 months
evidence.finding: Embedding skip connections and U-net skip connections were each part of successive speedrun world records.

expected_effect: About 0.01–0.03 nats, with negligible compute and parameter cost.
applicability: This is a scalar-only change and cannot break the parameter cap. It pairs naturally with the bigram card, which can use the same injection point. It is proven at 124M, and the mechanism does not depend on scale.
risks: Gains are only documented in combination with other speedrun tricks; no isolated ablation numbers were published. Lambdas can go negative, which is fine. Keep them out of weight decay: they are 1-D, so this happens automatically.
implementation:
In __init__: self.x_lam = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(n_layer)); self.x0_lam = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(n_layer)); self.skip_lam = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(n_layer//2)).
In forward: x0 = x; skips = []; half = n_layer//2; for i, blk in enumerate(self.blocks): if i >= half: x = x + self.skip_lam[i-half]*skips.pop(); x = self.x_lam[i]*x + self.x0_lam[i]*x0; x = blk(x); if i < half: skips.append(x). Popping gives the mirrored pairing.

name: Halve batch to 32×128 with β2 rescaled to a constant token half-life
current: batch 64 × 128 = 8,192 tokens/step, 15,000 steps, AdamW with default betas (0.9, 0.999), lr 3e-3. The run uses only about 48 of 146 wall-clock minutes.
proposal: batch_size=32, which doubles the steps to about 30,000. Set betas=(0.9, 0.9995), since β2* = 0.999^(64/32)^-1 ≈ 0.9995, to keep the second-moment half-life fixed in tokens. Scale lr by about 1/√2 to 2e-3 and keep warmup at the same token count (warmup_steps=800). Optionally scale β1 the same way (β1 = 0.9^(1/2) ≈ 0.949), which the paper also suggests.
mechanism: At a fixed token budget, below the critical batch size, more and smaller steps give more optimisation progress per token. Marek et al. show that the apparent penalty of small batches comes from keeping β2 fixed. Once the Adam averaging horizon is held constant in tokens, small batches match or beat large ones per FLOP and are more robust to hyperparameters.

evidence.source: Marek et al., Small Batch Size Training for Language Models (NeurIPS 2025, arXiv 2507.07101)
evidence.finding: Scaling rule β2* = β2^(B*/B), which holds the token half-life constant. Tested on a 30M model on FineWeb-Edu (600M tokens) and a 19M model on C4. Small batches are equal or better per FLOP and more robust, and with rescaled β2, batch sizes 16–32 match 128–256.

expected_effect: Probably about 0.01–0.04 nats. Wall time rises to about 60–75 min, still within the cap.
applicability: The paper's 30M-param FineWeb-Edu setup is almost exactly this one. There is about 3× wall-clock headroom, and the run is diagnosed as still improving, so extra optimiser steps are useful.
risks: Throughput per token drops on the L4 because small GEMMs use it less efficiently. This could combine badly with depth or width increases proposed in other cards; check the time budget. The lr needs a small sweep (1.5e-3 to 3e-3).
implementation: Hyperparameters: batch_size=32, lr=2e-3, warmup_steps=800. In build_optimizer: return AdamW(optim_groups, lr=args.lr, betas=(0.9, 0.9995)). If Muon (c1) is adopted, apply the β2 change only to the AdamW groups.
